canonical_topic: Local distribution networks and the citygate price
definition: Most end customers receive gas via a local distribution company's network of small pipes rather than directly from interstate pipelines; the retail price customers pay combines the citygate price (interstate-pipeline gas delivered to the local utility) plus a local delivery charge.
core_idea: Local distribution is expensive to maintain because it must connect every home and business regardless of individual profitability, so delivery charges — commonly about half of the total retail natural gas cost — make up a large share of what consumers pay.
key_points: Local distribution companies operate the network of small pipes that reach individual homes/businesses, distinct from interstate pipelines.
These networks must maintain universal connections regardless of profitability of any single connection, driving up maintenance costs.
Retail natural gas bills combine the citygate price (interstate-delivered gas price to the local utility) with a local delivery charge.
Local delivery charges commonly make up about half of the total retail cost of natural gas.
relationships: Citygate price sits downstream of the all-in/index/basis pricing structure described earlier, at the point interstate gas is handed to the local utility.
trading_implications: Retail price movements can be driven as much by local delivery-charge structure as by wholesale (index/basis) price movements.
caveats: Assuming the retail price consumers pay is just the wholesale (citygate) commodity price — roughly half is typically the local delivery charge.
